SUBDIVISION MAP ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St. · Sonoma

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law under the Subdivision Map Act, Government Code section 66410 et seq., as it may relate to real property at 123 Main St., Sonoma County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number 012-345-678), owned by Jane Doe, in connection with the following described land division: dividing a 10-acre parcel into three residential lots. It states what the Act provides about the statutory definition of "subdivision," when a tentative and final map (as opposed to a parcel map) is required, the Act's own listed exemptions including the lot line adjustment exemption, the statutory prohibition on selling, leasing, or financing land before a required map is recorded, how long an approved tentative map remains valid before it expires, and the requirement that an approved subdivision be consistent with the applicable general or specific plan. This information sheet is separate from, and does not substitute for, the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's own recording requirements for a condominium plan or declaration, the California Coastal Act's coastal development permit requirement, the common-law agreed-boundary doctrine that can fix an uncertain boundary line between adjoining owners without dividing a parcel, or any local subdivision ordinance, environmental review, or other permit that may separately apply to the same land. It does not tell Jane Doe or any other person whether the described land division is a "subdivision" under the Act, whether it qualifies for a statutory exemption, whether a tentative map, final map, or parcel map is required for it, or what to do next.

STATUTORY DEFINITION OF "SUBDIVISION"
The Subdivision Map Act applies to a "subdivision," a term the Act defines in its own definitions article rather than leaving to common usage. Government Code section 66424 defines "subdivision" as the division of a unit or units of land shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether the sale, lease, or financing is immediate or future. Parcels are treated as contiguous, and therefore as a single unit capable of being "divided," even where they are separated by a road, street, utility easement, or railroad right-of-way. The statutory definition also expressly reaches certain forms of ownership restructuring beyond a physical division of land: a condominium project, a community apartment project, and the conversion of five or more existing dwelling units to a stock cooperative are each included within "subdivision" by the statute's own terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Subdivision” means the division, by any subdivider, of any unit or units of improved or unimproved land, or any portion thereof, shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll as a unit or as contiguous units, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66424, Cal. Gov't Code § 66424 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66424.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the general definition in section 66424. It does not address the Act's separate exemption provisions (Government Code section 66412 and related sections), which remove specific categories of land division or ownership change from the Act's coverage even though they might otherwise fit this definition, nor does it determine whether any specific transaction described in this document falls within or outside the definition. A CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this definition returned a 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so no case law confirming or narrowing this statutory language is cited here.

WHEN A TENTATIVE AND FINAL MAP IS REQUIRED
The Act sets a numeric threshold, subject to listed exceptions, for when the more extensive tentative-and-final-map procedure applies rather than the simpler parcel map procedure. Government Code section 66426 requires a tentative and final map for a subdivision that creates five or more parcels, five or more condominiums, a community apartment project of five or more parcels, or a conversion to a stock cooperative of five or more dwelling units. The same section then lists six circumstances in which, even though a five-or-more-parcel subdivision is being created, a parcel map is required instead of the tentative-and-final-map procedure: among them, where the land before division is under five acres, each resulting parcel abuts a maintained public street, and the local legislative body requires no dedications or improvements; where each resulting parcel is 20 acres or more with approved access to a maintained public street; where the land is part of an industrial- or commercial-zoned tract with governing-body-approved street alignments; where each resulting parcel is at least 40 acres or a quarter of a quarter section; and where the division is solely to create an environmental subdivision under section 66418.2.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A tentative and final map shall be required for all subdivisions creating five or more parcels, five or more condominiums as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code, a community apartment project containing five or more parcels, or for the conversion of a dwelling to a stock cooperative containing five or more dwelling units, except where any one of the following occurs:"
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66426, Cal. Gov't Code § 66426 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66426.)
  "The land before division contains less than five acres, each parcel created by the division abuts upon a maintained public street or highway, and no dedications or improvements are required by the legislative body."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66426, Cal. Gov't Code § 66426(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66426.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the section 66426 threshold and its listed exceptions as written; it does not state which procedure applies to any property or transaction described in this document, and it does not address the separate, narrower parcel-map-only threshold that applies to subdivisions of four or fewer parcels under other sections of the Act, which this clause does not cover. A CourtListener search for case law was not completed because of an exhausted 125/day quota (429 rate-limit response); no judicial authority is cited here.

THE LOT LINE ADJUSTMENT EXEMPTION
The Act does not apply to every rearrangement of a boundary between parcels. Government Code section 66412(d) exempts a "lot line adjustment," defined for this purpose as an adjustment between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels where land taken from one parcel is added to an adjoining parcel and no greater number of parcels than originally existed is created, provided the local agency or advisory agency approves it. The statute limits that agency's review to whether the resulting parcels conform to the local general plan, any applicable specific plan or coastal plan, and zoning and building ordinances, and bars the agency from imposing conditions beyond that conformance check (with limited exceptions for prepayment of property taxes and utility relocation). The statute further provides that no tentative map, parcel map, or final map is required for a lot line adjustment, that the adjustment is instead reflected in a recorded deed, and that a record of survey is not required unless separately required by Business and Professions Code section 8762.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A lot line adjustment between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels, where the land taken from one parcel is added to an adjoining parcel, and where a greater number of parcels than originally existed is not thereby created, if the lot line adjustment is approved by the local agency, or advisory agency."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66412, Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66412.)
  "No tentative map, parcel map, or final map shall be required as a condition to the approval of a lot line adjustment."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66412, Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66412.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statutory lot line adjustment exemption in section 66412(d) only; it does not address the separate common-law agreed-boundary doctrine, which can also fix an uncertain boundary between adjoining owners but operates independently of this statute and does not require local agency approval. It also does not evaluate whether any specific line adjustment described in this document meets the four-or-fewer-parcels and no-net-increase conditions the statute states. CourtListener search results were not obtained (429 rate-limit error, 125/day quota exhausted), so no case law is cited on how courts have applied this exemption.

PROHIBITION ON SALE, LEASE, OR FINANCING BEFORE A REQUIRED MAP IS RECORDED
The Act backs its map requirements with a direct prohibition on certain transactions. Government Code section 66499.30(a) provides that no person shall sell, lease, or finance a parcel, or commence construction of a building for sale, lease, or financing on it (other than a model home), or allow occupancy of it, where a final map is required, until that final map has been filed for record by the county recorder; subdivision (b) states the same rule for a parcel map. Subdivision (c) separately prohibits conveying any part of a division of real property by parcel or block number or other designation until the required final or parcel map has been recorded. The statute qualifies this prohibition in two ways relevant here: subdivision (d) states that the prohibition does not apply to a parcel offered, contracted, sold, or leased in compliance with, or exempt from, the law regulating subdivision design and improvement in effect when the subdivision was established; and subdivision (e) states that the prohibition does not bar an offer or contract to sell, lease, or finance, or to construct improvements, where that sale, lease, financing, or construction is expressly conditioned on the approval and filing of the required final or parcel map. Subdivision (g) also tolls the limitation period for an enforcement action for any period during which there was no constructive notice of the violating transaction because no deed, lease, or financing document was recorded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No person shall sell, lease, or finance any parcel or parcels of real property or commence construction of any building for sale, lease or financing thereon, except for model homes, or allow occupancy thereof, for which a final map is required by this division or local ordinance, until the final map thereof in full compliance with this division and any local ordinance has been filed for record by the recorder of the county in which any portion of the subdivision is located."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66499.30, Cal. Gov't Code § 66499.30(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66499.30.)
  "Nothing contained in subdivisions (a) and (b) shall be deemed to prohibit an offer or contract to sell, lease, or finance real property or to construct improvements thereon where the sale, lease, or financing, or the commencement of construction, is expressly conditioned upon the approval and filing of a final subdivision map or parcel map, as required under this division."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66499.30, Cal. Gov't Code § 66499.30(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66499.30.)
  Known gap: This clause states the transactional prohibition and its own stated conditions and qualifications as written in section 66499.30; it does not state what legal effect, if any, a violation has on the validity of a deed or other conveyance actually made in violation of the section, since that consequence (if any) is not addressed within the text of this section itself and this clause does not rely on any other section or on case law to fill that gap. A CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this prohibition, including its effect on title, could not be completed because of an exhausted CourtListener quota (429 rate-limit response, 125/day limit); no case law is cited here.

HOW LONG AN APPROVED TENTATIVE MAP REMAINS VALID
An approved tentative map does not remain valid indefinitely. Government Code section 66452.6(a)(1) provides that an approved or conditionally approved tentative map expires 24 months after approval, or after any additional period prescribed by local ordinance not exceeding an additional 24 months, subject to a separate rule extending that period by 48 months per phased final map filing where the subdivider must spend at or above a stated, annually inflation-adjusted dollar threshold on off-site public improvements, up to a maximum of 10 years from approval. The statute separately provides, in subdivision (d), that once a tentative map expires, all proceedings on it terminate and no final map or parcel map covering any part of the land may be filed without first processing a new tentative map, although a filing made before expiration remains valid even if the local agency's subsequent processing, approval, or recording of it occurs after the expiration date. The statute also tolls the running of this period during a development moratorium (subdivision (b)), during litigation over the map's approval where the local agency grants a stay (subdivision (c)), and allows the subdivider to apply for a discretionary extension of up to six years in addition to the base period (subdivision (e)).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An approved or conditionally approved tentative map shall expire 24 months after its approval or conditional approval, or after any additional period of time as may be prescribed by local ordinance, not to exceed an additional 24 months."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66452.6, Cal. Gov't Code § 66452.6(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66452.6.)
  "The expiration of the approved or conditionally approved tentative map shall terminate all proceedings and no final map or parcel map of all or any portion of the real property included within the tentative map shall be filed with the legislative body without first processing a new tentative map."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66452.6, Cal. Gov't Code § 66452.6(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66452.6.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the expiration, tolling, and extension mechanics stated in section 66452.6 as written, including the version of the inflation-adjusted dollar threshold (currently stated as $236,790 in the fetched text) in effect on the date this text was fetched; because the statute itself directs that figure to be increased annually by a specified construction cost index, the current dollar amount at any later date will differ from the figure quoted and is not independently verified here. It does not address a vesting tentative map's separate statutory rules under a different article of the Act, which are not covered by this clause. CourtListener search results could not be obtained due to an exhausted 125/day quota (429 rate-limit error); no case law is cited on how courts have applied these expiration and tolling rules.

REQUIRED CONSISTENCY WITH THE GENERAL OR SPECIFIC PLAN
Approval of a subdivision under the Act is conditioned on a required local finding. Government Code section 66473.5 provides that no local agency may approve a tentative map, or a parcel map for which no tentative map was required, unless the legislative body finds that the proposed subdivision, together with its provisions for design and improvement, is consistent with the applicable general plan or any applicable specific plan. The statute further states that a proposed subdivision is consistent with such a plan only if the local agency has officially adopted the plan and the proposed subdivision or land use is compatible with the objectives, policies, general land uses, and programs the plan specifies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No local agency shall approve a tentative map, or a parcel map for which a tentative map was not required, unless the legislative body finds that the proposed subdivision, together with the provisions for its design and improvement, is consistent with the general plan required by Article 5 (commencing with Section 65300) of Chapter 3 of Division 1, or any specific plan adopted pursuant to Article 8 (commencing with Section 65450) of Chapter 3 of Division 1."
  — Cal. Gov. Code Section 66473.5, Cal. Gov't Code § 66473.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=66473.5.)
  Known gap: This clause states the consistency-finding requirement in section 66473.5 as written; it does not describe the separate substantive standards a general plan or specific plan itself must contain, nor does it evaluate whether any particular proposed subdivision described in this document would be found consistent with any particular jurisdiction's adopted plan. CourtListener search results could not be obtained (429 rate-limit error, 125/day quota exhausted), so no case law construing this consistency requirement is cited here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Jane Doe acknowledges having reviewed this information sheet describing California's Subdivision Map Act, Government Code section 66410 et seq., and understands that it states general California statutory law rather than a determination about 123 Main St. or about dividing a 10-acre parcel into three residential lots.

Signed at Santa Rosa, California.
